extracted.intended_audience: novelists, serious students of fiction, and critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting narrative method (first-person, third-person, epistolary, indirect approaches) and on dramatizing a character's consciousness; advice on economy and when to show vs tell. Uses examples (Harry Richmond, David Copperfield, Strether, Raskolnikov, Clarissa) to illustrate principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verisimilitude (fiction must look true)
rubrics_metrics.description: “fiction must look true, and there is no look of truth in inconsequence, and there is no authority at the back of a novel, independent of it, to vouch for the truth of its apparent wilfulness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inconsequence; ensure the novel produces its own authority and sense of truth from its internal coherence and causal/psychological plausibility rather than relying on external claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align method with the subject (portrait vs panorama)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book's method must suit its subject: e.g. Harry Richmond is 'to give the portrait of Harry Richmond' (the subject is the man), whereas Copperfield's subject is the phantasmagoria of the hero's life and the many people who populate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the story's core is a character's inner history or a broad social/panoramic scene; choose perspective and narrative devices that foreground that subject (portrait demands methods that render the central character; panorama may allow the narrator to remain primarily a reporter).

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person is useful when story is reflection of life outside narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: “a personal narrator will do very well and may be extremely helpful, so long as the story is only the reflection of life beyond and outside him”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person when the narrator's role is chiefly to describe and report the world and its people; it helps to know who is telling and makes the storyteller part of the story, enhancing pictorial reports of others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of first-person when story centers on narrator's inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: “as soon as the story begins to find its centre of gravity in his own life... his report of himself becomes a matter which might be strengthened, and which should accordingly give way to the stronger method.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the main weight of attention is the narrator's own consciousness and growth, first-person retrospective risks underpowering that inner life; prefer methods that make that consciousness immediately visible and enacted rather than merely reported (Meredith's Harry Richmond is cited as overtaxing autobiography).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer dramatization (showing) over reflection (telling) where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: “No reflection, no picture, where living drama is possible — it is a good rule; do not let the hero come between us and his active mind...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whenever the subject allows, render events, feelings, and thoughts as dramatic action rather than as after-the-fact description. Showing the mind 'in action' produces a straighter, more convincing effect for the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize consciousness: make the mind an onstage action
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of receiving a hero's report, present him 'in the act of judging and reflecting' so that 'his consciousness... is now before us in its original agitation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use techniques that expose the workings of a character's mind (free indirect style, focalization, scenes that enact thought-processes) so readers 'watch them absorbing' and can experience the mental life rather than rely solely on retrospective accounts (examples: Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov; James's Strether).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use third-person (or indirect methods) to show the hero's mind without authorial interposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist 'returns to the third person... but the difference is that instead of receiving his report we now see him in the act of judging and reflecting; his consciousness ... is now before us.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-person narrative can permit the reader to see a character's interiority dramatized without the limitations of autobiographical reporting; it retains the author's freedom while making a mind 'phenomenal' and observable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect method preferred: place the author at a remove to increase immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: “The prudent novelist tends to prefer an indirect to a direct method... The more circuitous procedure on the part of the author produces a straighter effect for the reader.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor narrative frames or focalizers that distance the authorial voice (e.g., telling the story through a character or dramatizing the mind) so the thing itself appears more directly to the reader; avoid overt authorial explanation when unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: push the chosen method only as far as the subject benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: “The method is to be pushed as far as the subject can profit by it, but no further... A story is damaged by too much treatment as by too little.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the nature of the subject indicate how much dramatization, introspection, or reportage is appropriate; avoid over-treating (which can displace the subject) or under-treating (which can leave it unsubstantial). Example: Dickens did not need to lay bare David's mind because the subject lay in the larger cast of characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Autobiographical device has intrinsic limits of objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: “no man can completely objectify himself, and a credible account of anything must appear to detach it, to set it altogether free for inspection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that retrospective first-person narration cannot fully 'objectify' internal states; where objectification or independent inspection of a mind is needed, choose methods that allow the reader to judge the subject without relying solely on the narrator's self-report.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary/diary as a device to dramatize immediacy of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a story of a series of letters or a day-by-day diary is 'engaged in the attempt to show a mind in action' and keeps emotion 'contemporaneous' and 'happening while she writes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use letters/diaries to create immediacy, recurring suspense, and the sensation of witnessing feeling as it occurs (Clarissa is cited); but be aware of practical and technical drawbacks—such methods strain plausibility and can be impracticable at large scale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator as a dramatic fact: make the storyteller a visible actor when useful
rubrics_metrics.description: “The figure of the story-teller is a dramatic fact... it is much more satisfactory to know who the story-teller is, and to see him as a part of the story.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the narrator's presence can enhance drama or authority, present them as an onstage element; yet avoid relying on their testimony for matters that need independent dramatization of inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let the subject determine the ideal point between showing and telling
rubrics_metrics.description: “For any story, no doubt, there is an ideal point upon this line of progress towards drama, where the author finds the right method of telling the story. The point is indicated by the subject of the story itself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the particular matter to be brought out and select the narrative approach (autobiography, epistolary, third-person dramatization, etc.) that best reveals that matter; the subject, not fashion, should guide method choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overt authorial claim: fathering the fiction upon another gives solidity
rubrics_metrics.description: “The fiction that he devises is ultimately his; but it looks poor and thin if he openly claims it as his... it becomes much more substantial as soon as he fathers it upon another.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative layering (presenting the story as belonging to a character rather than the author) to increase the work's perceived substance and coherence, while ensuring readers still have means to inspect and judge the material rather than accept it purely on authority.
